---
title: "Chapter 2: The Language of Mathematics"
subtitle: "Mathematical Language and Symbols"
toc: true
---

Unfamiliar notation can make mathematics appear more forbidding than it is.
Symbols do not conceal the underlying ideas; they express them economically
and with fewer ambiguities than ordinary prose often permits.

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YtERoY3nVl8
    title="Video introducing the language of mathematics" >}}

Like every language, mathematics has vocabulary, grammar, and conventions.
Its vocabulary consists of symbols and specialised terms. Its grammar tells us
which arrangements of symbols are meaningful. Its conventions allow different
readers to interpret the same notation consistently.

Mathematical language is valued because it is:

- **precise:** it allows distinctions that ordinary language may leave
  ambiguous;
- **concise:** it can communicate an idea using relatively few symbols; and
- **powerful:** it can describe complicated structures and relationships in a
  form that can be analysed logically.

These advantages do not mean that mathematical writing should consist only of
symbols. Good mathematical communication combines notation with clear prose.
The symbols compress the ideas; the surrounding words tell the reader what
those ideas mean and why they matter.

::: {.callout-note title="Learning outcomes"}
After completing this chapter, you should be able to:

- distinguish mathematical expressions, open sentences, and closed sentences;
- translate elementary statements between words and symbols;
- use common mathematical symbols and conventions correctly;
- apply the order-of-operations convention without treating PEMDAS
  mechanically;
- explain the elementary meanings of sets, relations, functions, and binary
  operations;
- interpret elementary logical connectives and quantifiers;
- distinguish a statement from its converse and its negation;
- explain how formality reduces ambiguity in mathematical communication; and
- recognise examples of these concepts in Biology and everyday life.
:::

## Expressions and sentences

The distinction between an **expression** and a **sentence** is similar to the
distinction between a noun phrase and a complete sentence in English.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition: mathematical expression"}
A **mathematical expression** is a well-formed arrangement of symbols that
represents a mathematical object, value, or quantity. An expression does not,
by itself, make a claim that can be judged true or false.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Definition: mathematical sentence"}
A **mathematical sentence** is a well-formed arrangement of symbols that makes
a mathematical assertion. A **closed sentence**, also called a
**proposition**, has a definite truth value: it is either true or false.
:::

An assertion whose truth depends on an unspecified variable is commonly called
an **open sentence**. Assigning the variable a value—or binding it with a
phrase such as “for every” or “there exists”—can turn it into a closed
sentence.

::: {.callout-tip title="Examples: expressions and sentences"}
| Notation | Classification | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| $b^2-4ac$ | expression | represents the discriminant of $ax^2+bx+c$ but makes no assertion |
| $m/V$ | expression | may represent density but makes no assertion |
| $x+1=2$ | open sentence | true only for particular values of $x$ |
| $1+1=2$ | true closed sentence | has a definite truth value |
| $1+1=3$ | false closed sentence | has a definite truth value |
| $\forall x\in\mathbb R,\ x^2\geq0$ | true closed sentence | the variable is bound by “for every” |
:::

Sentences often join expressions using relations such as
$=,\neq,<,\leq,$ and $\in$. The equality sign in $1+1=2$, for example,
asserts that the expressions on its two sides represent the same number.

## Reading and writing mathematical symbols

Symbols should be read as meaningful words or phrases, not as decorative
marks. The following are some common examples.

| Symbolic form | One way to read it |
|---|---|
| $x+y$ | the sum of $x$ and $y$ |
| $x-y$ | the difference between $x$ and $y$ |
| $xy$ | the product of $x$ and $y$ |
| $\dfrac{x}{y}$ | $x$ divided by $y$ |
| $x=y$ | $x$ is equal to $y$ |
| $x\neq y$ | $x$ is not equal to $y$ |
| $x<y$ | $x$ is less than $y$ |
| $x\leq y$ | $x$ is less than or equal to $y$ |
| $x\in A$ | $x$ is an element of $A$ |
| $A\subseteq B$ | $A$ is a subset of $B$ |
| $\forall x$ | for every $x$ |
| $\exists x$ | there exists an $x$ |
| $P\Rightarrow Q$ | if $P$ is true, then $Q$ is true |
| $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ | $P$ is true if and only if $Q$ is true |

### Translating between words and symbols

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: translating a temperature condition"}
Consider the sentence:

> The body temperature $T$ is at least $38^\circ\text{C}$.

The phrase **at least** includes $38$, so it can be written as

$$
T\geq38.
$$

The notation $T\geq38$ illustrates the three qualities introduced at the
beginning of this chapter:

- It is **concise** because it expresses the condition on body temperature
  using only a few symbols.
- It is **precise** once we have established that $T$ denotes temperature
  measured in degrees Celsius and that $\geq$ means “is greater than or equal
  to.” By contrast, “the body temperature is greater than
  $38^\circ\text{C}$” becomes $T>38$; removing the small bar excludes a
  temperature of exactly $38^\circ\text{C}$.
- It is **powerful** because it places the English sentence in a form that can
  readily be incorporated into calculations, compared with other
  inequalities, or manipulated using the rules of algebra.
:::

<details>
<summary><strong>Additional translation examples</strong></summary>

Here are further examples.

| Words | Symbols |
|---|---|
| $x$ is positive | $x>0$ |
| $n$ is no more than 20 | $n\leq20$ |
| $p$ is between 0 and 1, inclusive | $0\leq p\leq1$ |
| $x$ belongs to the set $A$ | $x\in A$ |
| $A$ and $B$ have no common elements | $A\cap B=\varnothing$ |
| there is a real number whose square is 4 | $\exists x\in\mathbb R\colon x^2=4$ |

Translation requires attention to meaning rather than word substitution. For
example, “less than” reverses the order in which quantities may appear:
“five less than $x$” is $x-5$, not $5-x$.

</details>

## Conventions in mathematical language

Mathematical conventions are agreed ways of writing and interpreting
mathematics. Without them, two readers could assign different meanings to the
same line of notation.

### Order of operations

One familiar convention is the order of operations, often remembered using
**PEMDAS**:

1. parentheses;
2. exponents;
3. multiplication and division; and
4. addition and subtraction.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: applying the order of operations"}

$$
\begin{aligned}
1+2-3(4+5)
  &=1+2-3(9) &&\text{parentheses}\\
  &=1+2-27   &&\text{multiplication}\\
  &=3-27     &&\text{addition from left to right}\\
  &=-24.     &&\text{subtraction}
\end{aligned}
$$

If we ignored the convention and performed the subtraction before the
multiplication, we would obtain a different result.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="PEMDAS is not simply a six-step ladder"}
Multiplication and division have the **same** precedence and are evaluated
from left to right. Addition and subtraction also have the same precedence
and are evaluated from left to right.

Thus,

$$
18\div3\times2=6\times2=12,
$$

not $3$. The letters M and D in PEMDAS do not mean that every multiplication
must be performed before every division.
:::

### Other common conventions

- If $n$ is a positive integer, then
  $x^n=\underbrace{x\cdot x\cdots x}_{n\text{ factors}}$.
- Symbols written next to one another usually indicate multiplication:
  $3x=3\cdot x$ and $ab=a\cdot b$.
- A fraction bar groups the entire numerator and denominator:
  $\dfrac{a+b}{c+d}$ means $(a+b)\div(c+d)$.
- Parentheses can change the object to which an operation applies:
  $-3^2=-(3^2)=-9$, whereas $(-3)^2=9$.
- The notation $f(x)$ usually means the value of the function $f$ at $x$; it
  does not ordinarily mean $f$ multiplied by $x$.
- The equality sign expresses sameness of value. Every expression in a chain
  such as $a=b=c$ must represent the same object.
- The approximation sign $\approx$ should be used when quantities are close
  but not exactly equal. For example, $\pi\approx3.14$, not $\pi=3.14$.

Conventions are not laws of nature. They are shared agreements that make
mathematical communication efficient and consistent.

## Four basic concepts

Four ideas appear repeatedly across mathematics: **sets**, **relations**,
**functions**, and **binary operations**. They provide a useful vocabulary for
describing collections of objects and the ways those objects are connected or
combined.

### Sets

::: {.callout-note title="Definition: set"}
For the purposes of this course, a **set** is a well-defined collection of
distinct objects. The objects belonging to the set are called its
**elements**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: set notation"}
Sets are usually denoted by capital letters and their elements by lowercase
letters. If

$$
A=\{\text{adenine},\text{cytosine},\text{guanine},\text{thymine}\},
$$

then $\text{adenine}\in A$, meaning that adenine is an element of $A$.

Repeated elements are not counted more than once, and the order in which
elements are listed does not matter:

$$
\{1,2,2,3\}=\{3,2,1\}=\{1,2,3\}.
$$
:::

If every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$, we write
$A\subseteq B$ and say that $A$ is a **subset** of $B$. The set with no
elements is the **empty set**, denoted by $\varnothing$.

Important operations on sets include

$$
A\cup B \quad\text{(union)},\qquad
A\cap B \quad\text{(intersection)}.
$$

The union contains elements that belong to $A$, to $B$, or to both. The
intersection contains only the elements common to both sets.

<details>
<summary><strong>Why this is called a naïve definition — non-examinable</strong></summary>

The definition above belongs to **naïve set theory** and is sufficient for this
course. In more advanced mathematics, allowing absolutely any verbal
description to define a set creates contradictions.

Russell's paradox considers the supposed set

$$
R=\{X:X\notin X\},
$$

the collection of all sets that are not elements of themselves. If $R\in R$,
then its defining property says $R\notin R$. But if $R\notin R$, then it
satisfies the defining property and therefore $R\in R$. Modern axiomatic set
theory carefully restricts how sets may be constructed to avoid this
contradiction. For now, treat this as an interesting piece of mathematical
trivia: the foundations of axiomatic set theory lie well beyond the scope of
this course.

</details>

### Ordered pairs and Cartesian products

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: ordered pairs and the Cartesian plane"}
An **ordered pair** $(a,b)$ records both its entries and their order. In
general, $(a,b)\neq(b,a)$. The **Cartesian product**

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b):a\in A\text{ and }b\in B\}.
$$

is simply the set of all possible pairs with $a\in A$ and $b\in B$. The
familiar Cartesian plane is

$$
\mathbb R\times\mathbb R=\mathbb R^2.
$$

Each point $(x,y)$ represents one element: $x$ gives its horizontal position
and $y$ its vertical position.
:::

### Relations

::: {.callout-note title="Definition: relation"}
A **relation from $A$ to $B$** is a subset of $A\times B$. It records which
elements of $A$ are related to which elements of $B$.
:::

Relations may also be defined on a single set. In an ecological network, for
example, “preys upon” is a relation on a set of species.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: a relation as a dietary model"}
Let

$$
A=\{\text{dog},\text{wolf},\text{hyena}\},
\qquad
B=\{\text{carnivore},\text{herbivore}\}.
$$

In a deliberately simplified model, allow the two dietary labels to overlap.
The resulting relation might be

$$
R=
\{
(\text{dog},\text{carnivore}),
(\text{dog},\text{herbivore}),
(\text{wolf},\text{carnivore}),
(\text{hyena},\text{carnivore})
\}.
$$

The dog has two outputs, so $R$ is not a function from $A$ to $B$. To remove
that ambiguity, introduce the mutually exclusive category “omnivore”:

$$
B'=\{\text{carnivore},\text{herbivore},\text{omnivore}\}.
$$

Define $f\colon A\to B'$ by

$$
f(\text{dog})=\text{omnivore},\qquad
f(\text{wolf})=\text{carnivore},\qquad
f(\text{hyena})=\text{carnivore}.
$$

The revised rule assigns every animal exactly one output and is therefore a
function. It is clearer for this task, although actual diets remain more
complicated. As Chapter 1 emphasised, models should be refined when their
simplifications become misleading.
:::

### Functions

::: {.callout-note title="Definition: function"}
A **function** $f$ from a set $A$ to a set $B$, written
$f\colon A\to B$, is a relation that assigns **every** element of $A$ to
**exactly one** element of $B$.
:::

The set $A$ is the **domain**, and $B$ is the **codomain**. The set of outputs
that the function actually produces is its **range**, which is a subset of the
codomain.

The phrase “exactly one” is essential. Different inputs may have the same
output, but one input cannot be assigned two different outputs by the same
function.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: DNA base pairing as a function"}
Let

$$
D=\{A,C,G,T\}
$$

be the set of DNA bases, where $A$ denotes **adenine**, $C$ denotes
**cytosine**, $G$ denotes **guanine**, and $T$ denotes **thymine**. These four
bases form part of the familiar double-helix structure shown below.

![An illustration of the DNA double helix. Image: [Institute for Molecular Bioscience, The University of Queensland](https://imb.uq.edu.au/dna-rna-genes-and-genomics-%E2%80%93-whats-difference).](images/dna-double-helix.jpg){#fig-dna-double-helix width=80%}

You may recall from high-school Biology that the two strands of DNA are held
together by specific complementary base pairing: adenine pairs with thymine,
while cytosine pairs with guanine. This pairing rule defines a function
$f\colon D\to D$ by

$$
f(A)=T,\qquad f(T)=A,\qquad f(C)=G,\qquad f(G)=C.
$$

Every input base has exactly one complementary base, so this rule is a
function.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="A common incomplete definition"}
It is not enough to say only that a function never assigns two different
outputs to the same input. A function $f\colon A\to B$ must also assign an
output to **every** element of its stated domain $A$.
:::

### Binary operations

::: {.callout-note title="Definition: binary operation"}
A **binary operation** on a set $A$ is a function

$$
\star\colon A\times A\to A.
$$

It takes two elements of $A$, combines them according to a rule, and produces
another element of $A$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Examples: binary operations and closure"}
Ordinary addition is a binary operation on the integers because the sum of
any two integers is another integer:

$$
+\colon\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z.
$$

Union is a binary operation on a collection of sets because the union of two
sets is again a set in that collection, provided the collection has been
chosen appropriately.

The choice of the underlying set matters. Subtraction is not a binary
operation on the positive integers because, for example, $2-3=-1$ is not a
positive integer. Division is not a binary operation on all real numbers
because division by zero is undefined.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: a custom binary operation"}
The symbol used for an operation acquires its meaning from its definition. It
need not represent one of the familiar operations. For example, define a new
operation $\star$ on the real numbers by

$$
a\star b=a+2b.
$$

We then calculate by applying the stated rule:

$$
3\star4=3+2(4)=11.
$$
:::

<details>
<summary><strong>Further example: associativity — non-examinable</strong></summary>

Nested operations must be evaluated carefully:

$$
(3\star4)\star2=11\star2=11+2(2)=15,
$$

whereas

$$
3\star(4\star2)=3\star8=3+2(8)=19.
$$

Thus, this particular operation is not associative. The example demonstrates
why we must read the definition of an unfamiliar symbol rather than assume
that it behaves like ordinary addition or multiplication.

</details>

## Elementary logic

Mathematical language is governed not only by conventions but also by
**logic**, the study of correct reasoning. Logic helps us combine statements
and determine what conclusions follow from them.

::: {.callout-note title="Scope of this section"}
The intention here is to give you a working familiarity with elementary
logic, not to provide a full course in symbolic or mathematical logic. You
should learn to read the basic logical connectives and quantifiers, interpret
simple logical statements, complete a basic two-variable truth table, and
distinguish a conditional statement from its converse.

Complicated truth tables involving many nested statements, formal proofs of
logical equivalence, and more advanced systems of logic lie beyond the scope
of this course unless explicitly stated otherwise.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Definition: proposition"}
A **proposition** is a closed sentence that is either true or false. It cannot
be both true and false under the same interpretation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: proposition versus non-proposition"}
“A dog is a mammal” is a proposition. The expression $x+1$ is not
a proposition because it makes no assertion, while the open sentence $x+1=2$
does not have a definite truth value until $x$ is specified or quantified.
:::

### Logical connectives

Simple propositions can be joined to form compound propositions. Let $P$ and
$Q$ denote propositions.

| Symbol | Name | Reading | When it is true |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\neg P$ | negation | not $P$ | when $P$ is false |
| $P\land Q$ | conjunction | $P$ and $Q$ | when both are true |
| $P\lor Q$ | disjunction | $P$ or $Q$ | when at least one is true |
| $P\Rightarrow Q$ | conditional | if $P$, then $Q$ | except when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false |
| $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ | biconditional | $P$ if and only if $Q$ | when $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth value |

In mathematics, **or** is normally inclusive: $P\lor Q$ is true when $P$ is
true, when $Q$ is true, or when both are true.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: a truth table for the logical connectives"}
A **truth table** displays the truth value of a compound proposition for every
possible combination of truth values of its parts.

| $P$ | $Q$ | $\neg P$ | $P\land Q$ | $P\lor Q$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | F | T | F | F |
| F | T | T | F | T | T | F |
| F | F | T | F | F | T | T |
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: a conditional and its converse"}
The conditional deserves particular attention. Let

- $P$ mean “the organism is a dog”; and
- $Q$ mean “the organism is a mammal.”

Then $P\Rightarrow Q$ says, “If the organism is a dog, then it is a mammal.”
Under the usual biological classification, this is true. Its **converse** is
$Q\Rightarrow P$: “If the organism is a mammal, then it is a dog.” The
converse is false because many mammals are not dogs.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Implication is not causation"}
The notation $P\Rightarrow Q$ means that whenever $P$ is true, $Q$ must also
be true. It does not by itself say that $P$ physically causes $Q$, nor does it
say that the converse $Q\Rightarrow P$ is true.
:::

### Quantifiers

Quantifiers tell us how many elements satisfy an open sentence.

| Symbol | Reading |
|---|---|
| $\forall$ | for every, or for all |
| $\exists$ | there exists at least one |
| $\exists!$ | there exists exactly one |

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: quantifying DNA base pairing"}
The DNA complementary-base function satisfies

$$
\forall x\in D,\qquad f(f(x))=x.
$$

This says that, for every DNA base $x$ in $D$, taking the complement twice
returns the original base.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: why the domain matters"}
The domain of a quantifier matters. The sentence

$$
\forall x\in\mathbb Z,\quad
\exists y\in\mathbb Z\text{ such that }x+y=0
$$

is true. Given any integer $x$, we may choose $y=-x$, which is also an
integer. The number $y$ is called the **additive inverse** of $x$.

By contrast, the sentence

$$
\forall x\in\mathbb N,\quad
\exists y\in\mathbb N\text{ such that }x+y=0
$$

is false when $\mathbb N$ denotes the natural or counting numbers. For
example, if $x=1$, the only real number satisfying $1+y=0$ is $y=-1$, and
$-1\notin\mathbb N$. The same equation therefore produces different truth
values when the permitted domain changes.
:::

<details>
<summary><strong>Biological extension: classification depends on the domain — non-examinable</strong></summary>

The same issue arises in biological classification. Consider the traditional
five-kingdom model, and let $\mathcal L$ be the set of living cellular
organisms covered by that model. Let

$$
\mathcal K=
\{
\text{Monera},
\text{Protista},
\text{Fungi},
\text{Plantae},
\text{Animalia}
\},
$$

where each kingdom is itself regarded as a set of organisms. We can express
the claim that every organism receives a kingdom classification as

$$
\forall x\in\mathcal L,\quad
\exists Y\in\mathcal K\text{ such that }x\in Y.
$$

Now suppose we broaden the domain to a set $\mathcal G$ containing all
biological entities that possess a genome, while leaving $\mathcal K$
unchanged. The corresponding claim

$$
\forall x\in\mathcal G,\quad
\exists Y\in\mathcal K\text{ such that }x\in Y
$$

is false because the enlarged domain includes viruses, which are not assigned
to any of the five kingdoms. The varicella-zoster virus—the virus that causes
chickenpox and shingles—is one counterexample: it has a
[double-stranded DNA
genome](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4066823/), but it does not
belong to Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, or Animalia. Defining the domain as
“entities possessing a genome” also avoids requiring us to settle the separate
and contested question of whether viruses should be called living.

This is another example of a mathematical model revealing its limits. The
quantified statement may be true for the domain the classification was built
to describe and false after that domain is enlarged.

</details>

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: negating quantified statements"}
Negating a quantified statement also changes its quantifier:

$$
\neg(\forall x,\ P(x))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists x\text{ such that }\neg P(x),
$$

and

$$
\neg(\exists x,\ P(x))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall x,\ \neg P(x).
$$

In words, the negation of “every organism has property $P$” is not “no
organism has property $P$.” It is the weaker statement “at least one organism
does not have property $P$.”
:::

Formal logic is not merely symbolic decoration. It structures reasoning,
helps us evaluate arguments, and allows explicitly stated rules to be
processed by computers. The following video illustrates that connection.

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5NGKbiA04Cw
    title="Video illustrating how computers use logical rules" >}}

## Formality in mathematical language

In ordinary conversation, context, tone, and shared experience often help us
interpret an incomplete or ambiguous sentence. Mathematics aims to reduce
that dependence on context. **Formality** means stating ideas in a sufficiently
structured way that their objects, assumptions, and logical relationships can
be interpreted consistently.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: formalising a classification rule"}
Consider the informal sentence:

> Each animal has one classification.

It does not identify the animals or classifications, and “one” may mean “at
least one” or “exactly one.” With $A$, $B'$, and $f$ defined by our dietary
model, the intended claim is

$$
\forall a\in A,\qquad
\exists! b\in B'\text{ such that }f(a)=b.
$$

This says that every animal receives exactly one classification. The words
define the objects; the notation makes the logical structure visible.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Making a statement sufficiently formal"}
Before presenting a mathematical claim, check that you have:

1. identified the objects being discussed;
2. defined the variables and their domains;
3. stated any assumptions;
4. used the required quantifiers and logical connectives; and
5. made clear exactly what is being asserted.

The appropriate degree of formality depends on the purpose and audience. A
classroom explanation may use more ordinary language than a formal proof, but
neither should rely on avoidable ambiguity.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Chapter summary"}
Sets identify the objects, relations connect them, functions assign outputs,
binary operations combine objects, and logic governs the statements we make
about them. Formality makes the objects, domains, assumptions, and conclusions
explicit. Symbols are useful only when we understand what they represent and
what they mean in the situation being studied.
:::

## Check your understanding

1. Classify each item as an expression, an open sentence, or a closed
   sentence:

   a. $3x+5$  
   b. $3x+5=20$  
   c. $3(5)+5=20$  
   d. $\forall x\in\mathbb R,\ x^2\geq0$

2. Translate each statement into symbols:

   a. The population $P$ is greater than 500.  
   b. The probability $p$ is between 0 and 1, inclusive.  
   c. Species $s$ belongs to the set $E$ of endangered species.

3. Evaluate the following and explain which convention you used at each step:

   $$
   20-12\div3\times2.
   $$

4. Let

   $$
   A=\{\text{cat},\text{dog},\text{eagle}\},
   \qquad
   B=\{\text{mammal},\text{bird}\}.
   $$

   Write a relation from $A$ to $B$ that records the biological class of each
   animal. Is your relation also a function? Explain.

5. Complete the following truth table. Then let $P$ mean “the organism is a
   dog” and $Q$ mean “the organism is a mammal”; write $P\Rightarrow Q$ and
   its converse in words.

   | $P$ | $Q$ | $\neg Q$ | $P\land\neg Q$ |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | T | T |  |  |
   | T | F |  |  |
   | F | T |  |  |
   | F | F |  |  |

6. Write the negation of each statement without simply placing the words “it
   is not true that” at the beginning:

   a. Every organism in the sample exhibits the trait.  
   b. There exists a patient whose temperature satisfies $T\geq38$.

<details>
<summary><strong>Additional practice</strong></summary>

1. Decide whether addition on $\mathbb Z$, subtraction on the positive
   integers, multiplication on $\mathbb R$, and division on $\mathbb R$ are
   binary operations.

2. Let $a\star b=a+2b$. Calculate $5\star(-2)$,
   $(1\star3)\star2$, and $1\star(3\star2)$. Is $\star$ associative?

3. Give a biological example of a set, a relation, and a function.

4. The sentence “Each specimen has one measurement” is ambiguous. List three
   pieces of information needed to make it a precise mathematical claim.

</details>

Choose one mathematical symbol that once seemed unfamiliar to you. Explain
